title: How South Korea Solved the Problem of Food Waste
paragraphs: Food waste is a major global problem. According to the United Nations Environment Programme, households and food businesses waste at least 1.05 billion tonnes of food every year, nearly a fifth of all the food available to consumers. However, South Korea has become an international example of how to deal with the problem, now recycling the vast majority of its food waste.

The situation used to be very different. In the 1990s, around 95% of South Korea's food waste went directly into landfills, and only about 2% was recycled. This caused serious problems for communities living near landfills, which suffered from unpleasant smells and liquid waste leaking from the sites. These communities began to campaign for change.

Over the following years, the government introduced a series of reforms. In January 2005, after building separate systems for collecting and treating food waste, South Korea banned the direct landfilling of food waste in urban areas. Then, in 2013, a "pay-as-you-throw" system for food waste was introduced across Seoul.

Under this system, households are charged according to how much food they throw away. Many people use special bins with electronic tags that weigh their food waste and record how much they need to pay. Kim Mi-Hwa, the chairperson of the Korean Zero Waste Movement Network, explained the principle simply: the more food waste you throw away, the more you pay. As a result, Seoul's food waste fell by almost a quarter. Today, about 95% of the country's food waste is recycled.

The Korean Zero Waste Movement Network, which brings together more than 180 environmental and consumer organizations, played a key role in these changes. In 2026, it was named a finalist for the Earthshot Prize, an international environmental award.

However, challenges remain. The amount of food waste per person is rising, treatment facilities are getting old, and some communities oppose new treatment sites. Kim warned that a high recycling rate should never become an excuse for producing more food waste. The network now hopes to help other Asian countries adopt similar systems.
